title: Bueno vs Bien: Good or Well in Spanish?
seo_title: Bueno vs Bien: Good or Well in Spanish?
meta_description: Bueno vs bien: when to use the adjective bueno and the adverb bien in Spanish, with estar bien, ser bueno, buen before nouns, common mistakes and a quiz.
excerpt: Adjective or adverb? A clear guide to good and well in Spanish.
body_html:
Bueno vs bien mirrors English “good” and “well”, but Spanish learners mix them up for a few specific reasons: bueno changes form (buen, buena, buenos), estar bien and ser bueno mean different things, and bueno is also a conversational filler. The basic rule is that bueno is an adjective that describes nouns, and bien is an adverb that describes verbs. Let’s turn that into real sentences.

Quick answer
  • Bueno/buena/buenos/buenas = good (adjective, describes nouns).
  • Bien = well, fine (adverb, describes verbs; never changes form).
  • Buen before a masculine singular noun: un buen libro.
  • Estoy bien = I’m fine. Está bueno = it tastes good (or, informally, he’s attractive).
{{toc}}

Bueno vs bien: the core rule

BuenoBien
Part of speechAdjectiveAdverb
DescribesNouns (people, things)Verbs (how something is done)
Changes form?Yes: buen, bueno, buena, buenos, buenasNo
ExampleEs una buena idea. It’s a good idea.Cantas muy bien. You sing very well.

The RAE dictionary notes that bueno shortens to buen before a masculine singular noun: buen día, buen trabajo.

When to use bueno

  • Es un buen profesor. He’s a good teacher.
  • Esta película es muy buena. This movie is very good.
  • Tengo buenas noticias. I have good news.
  • ¡Buenos días! Good morning!

Buen vs bueno

Before a masculine singular noun, drop the -o: un buen amigo. After the noun or a verb, keep it: un amigo bueno, El café es bueno. Feminine forms never shorten: una buena amiga.

When to use bien

  • Duermo bien. I sleep well.
  • ¿Estás bien? Are you okay?
  • Habla muy bien español. She speaks Spanish very well.
  • ¡Qué bien! How nice! / Great!
  • Lo pasamos bien. We had a good time.

That last one is a trap: English says “a good time”, but Spanish describes how you spent it, so it uses bien.

{{image:2}}

Ser bueno, estar bueno, estar bien

Combined with {{link:ser-vs-estar|ser and estar}}, these words change meaning:

PhraseMeaningExample
ser buenoto be good (quality, kindness, skill)Es buena persona. She’s a good person.
ser bueno en / parato be good atSoy bueno en matemáticas.
estar buenoto taste good; informally, to be attractiveLa sopa está buenísima.
estar biento be fine, okay, correctTodo está bien. Everything is fine.

Be careful with estar bueno about people: Ese actor está muy bueno means he’s very hot, not that he’s a good person. If you want to say someone is kind, use es buena persona.

{{book:love-slowly}}

Bueno as a filler word

In conversation, bueno works like “well”, “okay” or “anyway”:

  • Bueno, me voy. Okay, I’m off.
  • —¿Vienes? —Bueno, está bien. “Are you coming?” “Well, okay.”
  • ¿Bueno? Hello? (answering the phone in Mexico)

A quick mental shortcut

Ask “good what?” or “how?”. If you can answer “a good thing”, you need bueno. If you are describing how something happens or how someone feels, you need bien. So: una buena comida (a good meal) but comimos bien (we ate well).

Real conversations

  • A: ¿Qué tal el restaurante? (How was the restaurant?)
  • B: Muy bueno. La comida estaba buenísima y nos trataron muy bien. (Very good. The food was delicious and they treated us very well.)
  • A: ¡Qué bien! ¿Y el precio? (Great! And the price?)
  • B: Bueno… un poco caro, pero vale la pena. (Well… a bit expensive, but it’s worth it.)

Regional notes

Across the Spanish-speaking world, bueno and bien follow the same grammar, but everyday habits differ. In Mexico, people answer the phone with ¿Bueno?, which surprises visitors from Spain, where ¿Diga? or ¿Sí? is more usual. In parts of Latin America you will also hear bien used as an intensifier before adjectives, similar to muy: Está bien rico (It’s really tasty) or Es bien difícil (It’s really hard). This is informal and natural, but in formal writing stick with muy. In Spain, vale often takes the place of bueno when agreeing: —¿Quedamos a las ocho? —Vale.

Common mistakes

IncorrectCorrectWhy
Estoy bueno. (meaning “I’m fine”)Estoy bien.Estoy bueno means “I’m hot”
Hablas español muy bueno.Hablas español muy bien.Describes the verb: adverb
un bueno libroun buen libroShortens before masculine nouns
Lo pasamos bueno.Lo pasamos bien.Fixed expression with bien
Es bien persona.Es buena persona.Describes a noun: adjective
{{image:3}}

Try it yourself

  1. It’s a good day for a walk. (Es un buen día para pasear.)
  2. I don’t feel well. (No me siento bien.)
  3. This cake tastes really good. (Esta tarta está muy buena.)
  4. She’s good at languages. (Es buena para los idiomas.)
  5. Did you have a good time? (¿Lo pasaste bien?)

The same adjective-versus-adverb logic explains {{link:muy-vs-mucho|muy vs mucho}}. For more pairs, see {{link:spanish-confusing-words|my complete list of Spanish confusing words}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Bueno describes things and people; bien describes actions and states. Watch out for buen before masculine nouns, say estoy bien (never estoy bueno, unless you mean it), and enjoy using bueno as your new conversational “well”.

faq.q: What is the difference between bueno and bien?
faq.a: Bueno is an adjective meaning good and describes nouns. Bien is an adverb meaning well or fine and describes verbs or states.

faq.q: Is it estoy bien or estoy bueno?
faq.a: Estoy bien means I’m fine. Estoy bueno is informal for “I’m attractive”, so use estoy bien to say how you feel.
Before a masculine singular noun: un buen día, un buen amigo. Feminine forms like buena never shorten.

questions.explain: Before a masculine singular noun: buen.
Describes how he cooks: the adverb bien.
Pasarlo bien is the fixed phrase for having a good time.
